name: Urban Suite - Economic Disparity
catalogPath: Curricular Models/Urban Suite/Urban Suite - Economic Disparity
miniText: The scientific question is whether income-dependent location preferences reinforce residential and service inequality. In NetLogo's Urban Suite - Economic Disparity model, rich and poor entrants sample sites with different utility priorities, influence local price and quality, and attract jobs toward higher-value areas. The selected literature connects this mechanism to economic sorting and reinforcing land-use change: the acknowledged SOME ancestry confronts empirical requirements for residential development [1]; economic segregation models connect relocation choices with spatial inequality [2]; social context cautions against explaining observed separation from abstract preferences alone [3]. The source itself questions the assumption that jobs seek expensive land; binary income groups and directional neighborhood effects are propositions rather than established causal laws. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

modelSource.scientificOrigin: This model was loosely based on a model originally written by William Rand and Derek Robinson as part of the Sluce Project at the University of Michigan. For more about the original model (SOME) that was the basis for this model, please see: Brown D.G., Robinson D.T., Nassauer J.I., An L., Page S.E., Low B., Rand W., Zellner M., and R. Riolo (In Press) "Exurbia from the Bottom-Up: Agent-Based Modeling and Empirical Requirements." Geoforum. This model was developed during the Sprawl/Swarm Class at Illinois Institute of Technology in Fall 2006 under the supervision of Sarah Dunn and Martin Felsen, by the following group of students: Danil Nagy and Bridget Dodd. See http://www.sprawlcity.us/ for more details. Further modifications and refinements were made by members of the Center for Connected Learning and Computer-Based Modeling before releasing it as an Urban Suite model. The Urban Suite models were developed as part of the Procedural Modeling of Cities project, under the sponsorship of NSF ITR award 0326542, Electronic Arts & Maxis. Please see the project web site ([http://ccl.northwestern.edu/cities/](http://ccl.northwestern.edu/cities/)) for more information.
modelSource.notes: This is source research, not runtime execution or approval of the City Library reimplementation. Original model notices remain in the retained source.

verification.evidenceSummary: A recent article [Vinkovic D, Kirman A (2006) Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 103:19261–19265] showing that the Schelling model has a physical analogue extends our understanding of the model. However, prior research has already outlined a mathematical basis for the Schelling model and simulations based on it have already enhanced our understanding of the social dynamics that underlie the model, something that the physical analogue does not address. Research in social science has provided a formal basis for the segregative outcomes resulting from the residential selection process and simulations have replicated relevant spatial outcomes under different specifications of the residential dynamics. New and increasingly detailed survey data on preferences demonstrates the embeddedness of the Schelling selection process in the social behaviors of choosing alternative residential compositions.
